source_text: Hoc de consilio diffidentiae aut de studio aliter ineundae constitutionis induxerim, nisi ratio constiterit inprimis illa quod fides nostra obsequium apostolo debeat, prohibenti quaestiones inire, novis vocibus aures accommodare, haereticum post unam correptionem convenire, non post disputationem. Adeo interdixit disputationem, correptionem designans causam haeretici conveniendi, et hoc unam scilicet, quia non est Christianus, ne more Christiani semel et iterum et sub duobus aut tribus testibus castigandus videretur, cum ob hoc sit castigandus propter quod non sit cum illo disputandum, dehinc quoniam nihil proficiat congressio scripturarum, nisi plane ut stomachi qua ineat eversionem aut cerebri.
thought_title: Why heretics must not be given a debate over Scripture
orientation: Tertullian is explaining why he has decided to refuse heretics any dispute over the Scriptures, grounding this refusal in the apostle Paul's command.
pass_a_gloss: I would have introduced this from a plan of distrust or from a desire of entering upon the arrangement otherwise, unless that reason stood firm first of all, that our faith owes obedience to the apostle, who forbids entering upon questions, who forbids giving ears to new words, who forbids meeting with a heretic after one correction, not after a disputation. To such a degree he forbade disputation, designating correction as the cause of meeting with a heretic, and this one correction only, because he is not a Christian, lest he should seem to be chastised in the manner of a Christian once and again and under two or three witnesses, since for this reason he is to be chastised, because it is not to be disputed with him, and then because a contest of Scriptures accomplishes nothing, except plainly that it may enter upon the overturning of the stomach or of the brain.

choices.why: Keeps the genitive of quality literal, showing Tertullian's motive as distrust rather than a positive principle.

choices.english: a desire of entering upon the arrangement otherwise
choices.why: Preserves the gerundive phrase and the word 'aliter' (otherwise), which signals an alternative approach to the treatise's structure.
rejected: a wish to arrange things differently
a different plan for the work

choices.why: Keeps the legal force of 'debeat' (owes) and the dative 'apostolo', emphasizing obligation rather than mere respect.
rejected: should be obedient to the apostle

choices.why: Literal rendering of the idiom 'aures accommodare' (to lend ears) and 'novis vocibus' (new words), matching the Pauline warning against novel teaching.

choices.term: post unam correptionem convenire, non post disputationem
choices.english: meeting with a heretic after one correction, not after a disputation
choices.why: Keeps the contrast between 'correptio' and 'disputatio' and the force of 'post' with the accusative, showing the sequence Paul prescribes.

choices.term: stomachi qua ineat eversionem aut cerebri
choices.english: that it may enter upon the overturning of the stomach or of the brain
choices.why: Literal rendering of the vivid metaphor: disputation only upsets the stomach or brain, with 'eversio' kept as 'overturning' to preserve the physical image.
rejected: upset the stomach or the head

pass_b_english: I would not have introduced this from a plan of distrust, or from a desire of entering upon the arrangement otherwise, unless that principle stood first: our faith owes obedience to the apostle, who forbids entering into questions, giving ears to new words, and meeting with a heretic after one correction, not after a disputation. So thoroughly has he forbidden disputation that he designates correction as the reason for meeting with a heretic, and this once only, because he is not a Christian, lest he seem to be chastised in the manner of a Christian, once and again and under two or three witnesses, since he is to be chastised for this very reason: that there should be no disputing with him. And then, because a contest over the Scriptures profits nothing, except plainly that it may enter upon the overturning of the stomach or of the brain.

last_rejected.quote: who forbids entering into questions, giving ears to new words, and meeting with a heretic after one correction, not after a disputation
last_rejected.source_quote: prohibenti quaestiones inire, novis vocibus aures accommodare, haereticum post unam correptionem convenire, non post disputationem
last_rejected.why: 'non post disputationem' modifies 'convenire': meet a heretic after one correction, not after a debate. English attaches it to all three verbs.
last_rejected.fix: who forbids entering into questions, giving ears to new words, and meeting with a heretic after one correction, not after a disputation
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'non post disputationem' follows 'convenire', modifying only that verb; English placement is clear enough.

last_rejected.quote: So thoroughly has he forbidden disputation that he designates correction as the reason for meeting with a heretic
last_rejected.source_quote: Adeo interdixit disputationem, correptionem designans causam haeretici conveniendi
last_rejected.why: 'correptionem' is correction/rebuke, but the point is he designates rebuke (not disputation) as the cause for meeting. English loses the contrast.
last_rejected.fix: So thoroughly did he forbid disputation, designating rebuke as the reason for meeting with a heretic
last_rejected.ruling: Translation captures that correction, not disputation, is the designated cause for meeting the heretic.
